mcqs.question: Why does a single stalled instruction (e.g., a cache-missing load) hurt an in-order pipeline more than an out-of-order one?
options: In-order pipelines have fewer functional units than out-of-order pipelines
In an in-order pipeline the stall blocks every instruction behind it in program order, even ones with no dependence on the stalled instruction, while OoO lets independent instructions bypass it
In-order pipelines cannot execute load instructions at all
Out-of-order pipelines never experience cache misses
mcqs.explanation: In-order issue means instructions can't pass a stalled instruction ahead of them even if fully independent, wasting available parallelism; OoO execution specifically exists to let independent later instructions execute while an earlier one waits. Functional unit count and load support are unrelated, and OoO cores absolutely still experience cache misses.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of a reservation station in an out-of-order core?
options: To permanently store the architectural register file's contents
To hold an issued instruction and its operands (or placeholders for pending ones) until all operands are ready, decoupling when it's fetched from when it executes
To translate virtual addresses to physical addresses before a memory access
To predict whether a branch will be taken or not taken
mcqs.explanation: Reservation stations let an instruction issue immediately and wait for its operands there, freeing the front end to keep fetching rather than stalling. Address translation is the MMU/TLB's job and branch direction prediction is a separate predictor structure, not a reservation station's role.

mcqs.question: Why does an out-of-order core need a reorder buffer (ROB) even though execution itself happens out of program order?
options: To make instructions execute faster by skipping the decode stage
To ensure results commit to architectural state in original program order, so exceptions stay precise and software never observes out-of-order effects
To store the branch predictor's history table
To replace the need for reservation stations entirely
mcqs.explanation: The ROB lets execution proceed out of order internally while guaranteeing commit — the point where results become visible to architectural state — happens strictly in program order, which is what precise exceptions require. It doesn't speed up decode, isn't a predictor structure, and works alongside reservation stations, not instead of them.
